title: The Red Sea: Between Two Continents
summary: How the Red Sea sits inside a slowly widening crack between the African and Arabian plates, and why its water is some of the saltiest and warmest on Earth.
poll: Two continents are slowly pulling apart underneath the Red Sea.

versions.title: A Sea Between Two Lands
versions.text:
The Red Sea is a sea. It is long. It is narrow too. Africa is on one side. Arabia is on the other side.

Long ago, Earth was one land. It broke into big parts. Each part is a continent. Big rock slabs hold up the land. Each slab is a plate.

The sea sits in a long crack. The crack splits two plates. The plates pull apart. So the crack grows a bit each year. This takes a long time.

Not many rivers flow in. The sun is hot. It dries the sea fast. Salt stays in the sea. So the sea is very salty.

The sea stays warm all year. Fish like the warm, salty water. Coral likes it too.

Scientists look at rocks on the sea floor. They study the crack.

In time, the crack may grow big. Then the sea could turn into a new ocean. Africa and Arabia would be far apart.

versions.title: A Sea Between Two Lands
versions.text:
The Red Sea is a long, narrow sea. It lies between two lands. One side is Africa. The other side is Arabia.

Long ago, Earth's crust broke into big parts. Each big part is a continent. Continents sit on top of rock slabs called plates. The plates can move, but very slowly.

The Red Sea lies in a long crack. The crack is where two plates meet. One is the African plate. One is the Arabian plate. Bit by bit, the two plates pull apart. So the crack gets wider each year.

Few rivers flow into the Red Sea. The hot sun dries up the water fast. When water dries up, it leaves salt behind. That is why the Red Sea is one of the saltiest seas on Earth.

The Red Sea stays warm most of the year. Its warm, salty water is a fine home for coral and fish.

Scientists study rocks on the sea floor. The rocks show that the crack is still growing.

Far off in time, the crack may grow so wide that the Red Sea turns into a brand-new ocean.

versions.title: The Red Sea: Between Two Continents
versions.text:
The Red Sea stretches between Africa and Arabia. Its water is warm, salty, and clear. It lies inside a long, narrow basin.

Earth's outer crust is not one solid shell. Instead, it is broken into huge, moving pieces. Each huge piece of land is a continent. Continents ride on top of big rock slabs called plates. These plates move all the time, but very slowly.

The Red Sea sits inside a long, deep crack. The crack formed where the African plate and the Arabian plate meet. Little by little, the two plates have pulled apart. Because of this slow movement, the crack keeps growing wider.

Very few rivers flow into the Red Sea. A hot desert sun beats down on it nearly every day. This heat makes the seawater dry up fast. When water dries up, it leaves salt behind. For this reason, the Red Sea is one of the saltiest seas on the planet.

The Red Sea also stays warm all year, even in winter. Its clear, salty water is home to coral and many fish.

Scientists study rocks on the sea floor. These rocks show how fast the crack is growing.

Many scientists think that, far in the future, this crack could grow wide enough to turn the Red Sea into a brand-new ocean.

versions.title: The Red Sea: Between Two Continents
versions.text:
The Red Sea stretches between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, and Saudi Arabia has a long coast along its eastern side. The sea is long, narrow, warm, and salty.

Scientists call the study of Earth's moving crust plate tectonics. Earth's outer shell is broken into huge, slowly shifting pieces called plates. Each huge piece of land riding on a plate is a continent.

The Red Sea fills a basin, a bowl-shaped dip in Earth's crust. This basin sits inside a rift, where the African plate and the Arabian plate meet. When the two plates pull apart, the rift grows a little wider. Bit by bit, over millions of years, the rift widens and the basin grows.

Very few rivers flow into the Red Sea, and the desert sun is strong nearly every day. The heat makes seawater evaporate, and when water evaporates, it leaves salt behind. For this reason, the Red Sea is one of the saltiest seas on Earth.

The Red Sea also stays warm all year, even in winter. Its warm, clear, salty water is a fine home for coral and many kinds of fish.

Scientists who study the rift have found young rock rising along its center. This is a sign that the plates are still pulling apart today.

Many geologists predict that the widening rift could one day grow so wide that the Red Sea becomes a brand-new ocean.

versions.title: The Red Sea: Between Two Continents
versions.text:
The Red Sea stretches between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, and Saudi Arabia has a long coastline along its eastern side. The sea is long, narrow, warm, and salty. Beneath its surface lies one of the most active rift zones on the planet.

Scientists call the study of Earth's moving crust plate tectonics. Earth's crust may look like one solid shell, but it is actually broken into huge, moving pieces called plates. Each huge piece of land riding on a plate is called a continent. Most plates move only a few centimeters each year, far too slowly to feel.

The Red Sea fills a basin, a bowl-shaped dip in Earth's crust. This basin sits inside a rift, a giant crack in Earth's crust. The rift is where the African plate and the Arabian plate meet. When the two plates pull apart, the rift grows slightly wider. Little by little, over millions of years, the rift widens and the basin grows larger.

Very few rivers empty into the Red Sea, and the desert sun blazes down nearly every day of the year. This heat makes seawater evaporate quickly, and when water evaporates, it leaves salt behind. For this reason, the Red Sea ranks among the saltiest seas on the planet.

The Red Sea also stays remarkably warm throughout the year, even during winter, because it lies in a hot, dry part of the world. Its warm, clear, salty water is an excellent home for colorful coral and countless kinds of fish.

Geologists who study the rift have discovered young rock rising along its center, a sign that the two plates are still pulling apart today.

More than a thousand kinds of fish live in the Red Sea, and its warm water helps many kinds of coral flourish there as well.

Many geologists predict that this widening rift could eventually grow large enough to turn the Red Sea into a brand-new ocean. If that happens, Africa and Arabia will stand much farther apart than they do today.

versions.title: The Red Sea: Between Two Continents

versions.title: A Sea Being Born: The Red Sea Rift
versions.text:
The Red Sea is a long, narrow sea that separates two continents, with Africa lying along its western margin and the Arabian Peninsula, home to Saudi Arabia, along its eastern margin.

The science of plate tectonics explains how Earth's rigid outer crust moves. It is divided into huge, slowly shifting plates. Their motion reshapes continents over long spans of time.

The Red Sea occupies a rift valley, a long depression that forms where two plates meet along a fault. A fault is a crack in Earth's crust along which rock on either side can shift. Here, the African plate and the Arabian plate are slowly moving apart.

This rift forms part of a much larger system of rifts that extends south into East Africa, a region geologists consider among the most active on the planet.

As the two plates separate, the basin holding the Red Sea steadily widens, even though this motion amounts to only a few centimeters each year. Over millions of years, this slow process has shaped the sea into its present form.

Geologists who study the seafloor have found young volcanic rock rising along the center of the rift, further evidence that the plates are still spreading apart today.

Very few rivers flow into the Red Sea, and an intense desert sun drives constant evaporation. Because so much water evaporates while so little fresh water flows in, the sea's salinity, the amount of salt dissolved in water, ranks among the highest of any sea on Earth.

The Red Sea also stays unusually warm all year, even in winter, conditions that support vibrant coral reefs and a wide range of marine life.

Many geologists predict that this widening rift could eventually grow large enough to transform the Red Sea into an entirely new ocean, and studying this process helps scientists understand how brand-new oceans are born.

versions.title: A Sea Being Born: The Red Sea Rift
versions.text:
The Red Sea is an elongated, comparatively narrow body of water separating two continents, flanked by Africa along its western margin and by the Arabian Peninsula, home to Saudi Arabia, along its eastern margin, and its unusual shape and location are no accident of geography but rather the direct product of ongoing geologic forces.

According to the science of plate tectonics, Earth's rigid outer crust is divided into immense, slowly shifting plates whose gradual motion reshapes continents across vast, almost unimaginable spans of geologic time. The Red Sea occupies a rift valley, an elongated depression that forms where two plates meet along a fault, a fracture across which rock on either side can shift relative to the other, and here the African plate and the Arabian plate are slowly diverging from one another, a process that has been underway for tens of millions of years. This rift constitutes part of a considerably larger rift system extending southward into East Africa, widely regarded by geologists as one of the most geologically active regions found anywhere on the planet.

As the two plates continue to separate, the basin containing the Red Sea steadily widens and deepens, even though the underlying motion amounts to merely a few centimeters annually; across millions of years, however, this persistent tectonic activity has gradually shaped the sea into its present form, and geologists examining the seafloor have discovered young volcanic rock rising along the center of the rift, offering further corroborating evidence of ongoing spreading beneath the waves.

Remarkably few rivers empty into the Red Sea, while an intense desert sun beats down relentlessly upon its surface for nearly every day of the year, driving continuous, large-scale evaporation that far outpaces any inflow of fresh water. Because so much water evaporates while comparatively little fresh water flows in to replace it, the sea's salinity, the concentration of dissolved salt within its water, ranks among the highest ever recorded in any sea on Earth, a fact that fascinates scientists who study ocean chemistry.

The Red Sea likewise remains unusually warm throughout the entire year, even during the winter months, conditions that sustain vibrant coral reefs and an extraordinary degree of marine biodiversity along its shores.

Many geologists predict that this continually widening rift could eventually expand sufficiently to transform the Red Sea into an entirely new ocean, gradually pushing Africa and Arabia considerably farther apart than they presently stand, much as an earlier rift once separated other landmasses long ago.

versions.title: A Sea Being Born: The Red Sea Rift
versions.text:
The Red Sea is an elongated, comparatively narrow body of water separating two continents, flanked by Africa along its western margin and by the Arabian Peninsula, home to Saudi Arabia, along its eastern margin, and its distinctive shape and location are no accident of geography but rather the direct, ongoing product of immense geologic forces operating far beneath its waves.

According to the science of plate tectonics, Earth's rigid outer crust is divided into immense, slowly shifting plates whose gradual motion continuously reshapes continents across vast, almost unimaginable spans of geologic time. The Red Sea occupies a rift valley, an elongated depression that forms where two plates meet along a fault, a fracture across which rock on either side can shift relative to the other, and here the African plate and the Arabian plate have been slowly diverging from one another for tens of millions of years. This rift constitutes part of a considerably larger rift system extending southward into East Africa, widely regarded by geologists as among the most geologically active regions found anywhere on the planet, and one that offers researchers an exceptionally clear window into how oceans are born.

As the two plates continue to separate, the basin containing the Red Sea steadily widens and deepens, even though the underlying motion amounts to merely a few centimeters annually; across millions of years, nevertheless, this persistent tectonic activity has gradually shaped the sea into its present form, and geologists examining the seafloor have discovered young volcanic rock rising along the center of the rift, offering further corroborating evidence of ongoing spreading beneath the waves.

Remarkably few rivers empty into the Red Sea, while an intense desert sun beats down relentlessly upon its surface for nearly every day of the year, driving continuous, large-scale evaporation that far outpaces any inflow of fresh water from the surrounding land. Because so much water evaporates while comparatively little fresh water flows in to replace it, the sea's salinity, the concentration of dissolved salt within its water, ranks among the highest ever recorded in any sea on Earth, a phenomenon that continues to fascinate scientists who study ocean chemistry and climate.

The Red Sea likewise remains unusually warm throughout the entire year, even during the winter months, conditions that sustain vibrant coral reefs and an extraordinary degree of marine biodiversity along its shores.

Many geologists predict that this continually widening rift could eventually expand sufficiently to transform the Red Sea into an entirely new ocean, gradually pushing Africa and Arabia considerably farther apart than they presently stand, much as an earlier ancient rift once separated other landmasses over the immense course of Earth's geologic history.

keyWords.example: Scientists use maps to show where each plate lies.

keyWords.example: A crack ran across the dry ground after the rain stopped.

keyWords.definition: not wide; thin from side to side

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How the Red Sea sits in a crack between two continents that are slowly moving apart
How ships cross the Red Sea to trade goods and spices in the east and the west
How many kinds of fish live in the Red Sea, in its reefs and in its deep water
How people built cities next to the Red Sea, such as ports, towns, and old camps
questions.why: The article explains that the Red Sea lies in a crack between Africa and Arabia and why that makes its water salty and warm.

wrong.B: The article does not describe ships trading goods.
wrong.C: The article does not list kinds of fish.
wrong.D: The article does not talk about building cities.

questions.stem: What is a continent?
options: A tiny sea animal
A huge piece of land on Earth
A kind of salty rock
A deep crack in the sea floor
questions.why: In the article, Earth's land broke into huge parts, and each huge part is a continent.

wrong.A: The article does not talk about sea animals.
wrong.C: A continent is land, not a kind of rock.
wrong.D: A crack is where plates meet, not a continent.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is a plate?
options: A dish used on a ship to serve hot food to sailors
A kind of fish found in the Red Sea near reefs
A small, narrow island far from the coast
A huge, hard slab of rock that continents sit on
questions.why: In the article, the land sits on huge slabs of rock, and each slab is called a plate.

wrong.A: The article is not about dishes.
wrong.B: The article does not describe fish here.
wrong.C: An island is land with water around it, not a plate.

questions.stem: In the article, narrow means
options: Very wide, like an ocean
Very deep, like a canyon
Thin from side to side
Completely full of salt
questions.why: The article describes the Red Sea as a long, narrow sea, meaning it is thin from side to side.

wrong.A: Narrow means the opposite of wide.
wrong.B: Narrow describes width, not how deep the sea is.
wrong.D: That describes salty, a different word in the article.

questions.stem: If the crack between Africa and Arabia keeps getting wider for millions of years, what will most likely happen?
options: The Red Sea will dry up completely
Africa and Arabia will join into one piece of land
The sea will become a lake with no salt
The Red Sea could grow into a whole new ocean
questions.why: In the article, the crack may grow so wide that the Red Sea turns into a huge new ocean.

wrong.A: The article says the sea grows wider, not that it dries up.
wrong.B: The plates are pulling apart, not joining together.
wrong.C: The article says the sea is very salty, not that it loses its salt.

questions.stem: The article says the crack keeps getting a little wider every year. What does this tell us about the two plates?
options: They are slowly moving away from each other
They are still and never move
They are melting into the sea
They are moving slowly toward each other

wrong.B: If the plates never moved, the crack would not get wider.
wrong.C: The article does not say the plates melt.
wrong.D: Plates moving toward each other would make the crack smaller, not wider.

questions.stem: Why did the author most likely write this article?
options: To teach readers how to swim safely in the sea and stay near the shore
To describe a trip the author took on a ship across the water
To help readers understand why the Red Sea formed the way it did
To compare the Red Sea to a famous lake in another country
questions.why: The article mainly explains how the Red Sea sits in a widening crack and why its water is salty and warm.

wrong.A: The article does not teach swimming.
wrong.B: No ship trip is described.
wrong.D: No lake is compared to the Red Sea.

options: Many big rivers flow in and add extra salt to it
Hot sun dries the water, leaving salt behind
Fish release extra salt into the water constantly
People add extra salt to keep ships afloat
questions.why: The article explains that the hot sun dries up water quickly and very few rivers add fresh water, so salt stays behind.

wrong.C: The article does not mention fish adding salt.
wrong.D: The article does not say people add salt.

I told why the Red Sea is salty and warm.

MID.prompt: Explain how moving tectonic plates and a hot, dry climate together shape the Red Sea. Use at least three details from the article.
checklist: I explained how the rift and basin are changing.
I explained why the sea is so salty and warm.
I used at least three details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: The Red Sea sits inside a rift, a deep crack where the African and Arabian tectonic plates are slowly pulling apart, which causes the basin holding the sea to steadily widen and sink lower over millions of years. At the same time, a powerful desert sun causes huge amounts of water to evaporate while very few rivers flow in to replace it, leaving behind salt and making the Red Sea one of the saltiest and warmest seas on Earth. Many geologists predict that the widening rift could eventually turn the Red Sea into a brand-new ocean.

keyWords.definition: the branch of science that studies the huge plates of Earth's crust and how they move

keyWords.definition: the process by which a liquid changes into vapor, usually from heat

keyWords.definition: a scientist who studies rocks, Earth's crust, and how the planet changes over time

keyWords.definition: a crack in Earth's crust along which rock on either side can shift

HIGH.prompt: Explain how plate tectonics causes both the Red Sea's widening and its extreme salinity, citing evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained the tectonic cause of the widening rift.
I explained why evaporation and few rivers raise salinity.
I cited evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Plate tectonics explains both the Red Sea's widening and its high salinity. The African and Arabian plates are slowly diverging along a fault within a rift valley, and geologists point to young volcanic rock at the center of the rift as evidence that this tectonic spreading is still active, steadily widening and deepening the basin. At the same time, this same desert setting produces intense evaporation while very little fresh water flows in, so the sea's salinity ranks among the highest on Earth, and geologists predict the rift's widening could eventually transform the Red Sea into an entirely new ocean.
